BSAIC-09
The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open with the claim that strategy lives and dies in the operating model. An AI strategy the operating model cannot execute is a document, not a strategy, and the session exists to make the execution discipline visible and teachable.
Introduce the AI operating model archetypes. Define a centralised Centre of Excellence as the pattern in which AI capability is concentrated for leverage and consistency, a federated model as the pattern in which business units own their own AI capability for pace and relevance, and a hybrid model as the attempt to combine the two through a shared platform and distributed delivery. Walk through the decision logic that points to each archetype and show named examples from the banking, retail, and industrial sectors.
Move to RACI matrix design. Show how decision rights in AI systems span data stewards, model owners, business sponsors, and risk functions, and how a poorly designed RACI produces the characteristic AI failure mode of an incident with no accountable owner. Work through a RACI for an AI model that makes a materially impactful decision, and make the accountabilities concrete.
Cover process redesign for AI integration. Identify the human decision nodes that AI can inform, augment, or replace, and show how the redesign is not a one-to-one substitution but a rethinking of the process itself. Use a credit-decisioning or demand-forecasting example to make the redesign visible.
Address cross-functional teaming. Define the composition and charter of an effective AI product team: the technical lead, the domain expert, the risk representative, the product owner, and the business sponsor. Show how charter confusion produces team dysfunction and how explicit decision rights prevent it.
Close the content with change management. Role displacement, capability gaps, and resistance to new accountability structures are the predictable human responses to operating model redesign. Name the specific interventions, coaching, communication, and capability development, that the literature shows to be effective, and connect them to the work done in the Leadership workstream.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to architect a target operating model that specifies decision rights and the interface between centralised and federated functions, trace the dependencies between use cases, processes, and roles to identify where current choices will constrain scaling, and make a reasoned case for a CoE, federated, or hybrid pattern with explicit trade-offs in accountability and pace.
"

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open with the observation that most enterprise AI portfolios resemble a shopping list more than a strategy. The shopping-list portfolio has a technical name, a portfolio of point solutions without foundational investments, and the failure mode it produces is well documented and expensive.
Introduce AI project interdependencies and foundational-capability sequencing. Investments in data platforms, MLOps infrastructure, identity and access management, and model governance enable and gate downstream use cases. Show a concrete example where three downstream use cases all depended on the same absent foundational investment, and the portfolio delivered only one of them because the others were starved of the prerequisite. Introduce the sequencing discipline of quick wins, capability builders, and flagship transformations, arranged so that each phase unlocks the next.
Move to risk-adjusted portfolio scoring. Walk through a multi-criteria prioritisation matrix that incorporates technical debt, regulatory exposure, talent availability, data readiness, and strategic alignment. Show the weighting trade-offs that differ by industry and by the organisation's position on its maturity curve, and connect this to the maturity model work in BSAIC-16. Make explicit the difference between scoring for comparison and scoring for decision, and why the scoring instrument itself needs to be calibrated before it is trusted.
Address the staged investment logic. Quick wins build credibility and release resources, capability builders remove the foundational constraints that gate the rest of the portfolio, and flagship transformations deliver the strategic intent. Show how mis-sequencing produces programme failure even when each individual project is well managed.
Explore the communication discipline. Translating a technical sequencing logic into a Board-ready investment narrative is a specialist act. Walk through the narrative structure: the strategic frame, the dependency map, the staged investment ask, and the forward-looking risk posture. Contrast this with the project-by-project approval pattern that produces portfolio incoherence.
Close the content with the failure modes. Approving point solutions without their prerequisites, neglecting dependencies, under-investing in foundational capabilities, and substituting a list of initiatives for a coherent roadmap. Name each and the specific preventive discipline.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to curate a risk-adjusted portfolio that sequences quick wins, capability builders, and flagship transformations, rank-order initiatives against a defensible multi-criteria instrument, trace foundational dependencies and diagnose the point-solution failure mode, and communicate the roadmap to a simulated Board as an investment narrative that survives cross-examination.
"

The materials of this learning event are available under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open by naming the central design choice. Every AI deployment makes a decision about where humans and machines sit on the work, and most organisations make that decision implicitly, by default, rather than by design. The session exists to make it a deliberate act.
Introduce the augmentation-automation spectrum. Define augmentation as AI supporting a human whose judgement remains primary, and automation as AI executing without routine human involvement. Anchor the discussion in the theoretical foundations from Brynjolfsson and McAfee, and show how current enterprise practice has evolved the spectrum into a more granular set of design patterns.
Move to task decomposition methodology. Show how a role breaks down into tasks, and each task into subtasks, and how each subtask can be assessed for where value sits on the human-machine boundary. Use a knowledge-work role, legal document review, radiology, or financial analysis, and walk through the decomposition in detail. Make the exercise concrete, not theoretical.
Introduce cognitive load theory as the design constraint that most human-AI systems ignore. Working memory is finite, and poorly designed AI interfaces overwhelm practitioners with alerts, recommendations, and probabilistic scores that cannot be usefully integrated. Show how interfaces that respect cognitive load, by summarising rather than streaming and by prioritising rather than enumerating, produce measurably better outcomes.
Work through organisational case studies. Radiological diagnosis, where AI augments the radiologist's reading, legal document review, where AI pre-filters and classifies, and financial analysis, where AI triangulates signals across noisy sources. Make clear what worked, what did not, and what the design choices were that differentiated the outcomes.
Close the content with measurement. Productivity metrics alone are insufficient because they miss decision quality and practitioner wellbeing. Walk through the full measurement stack and show why a single-metric view produces gaming and burnout, both of which defeat the deployment's original purpose.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to deconstruct a knowledge-work role into its constituent tasks and map each against the augmentation-automation spectrum with reference to complementarity and cognitive-load evidence, design a human-AI dyad that specifies task division, support form, and oversight interface, and contest the implicit assumptions behind a proposed automation design about where value and risk sit on the human-machine boundary.
"

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
0 - 10 minutes
- Introduce real-world examples of AI in healthcare (e.g., diagnosis, risk prediction)
- Motivate the need for AI in clinical decision-making
- Discuss why healthcare problems are fundamentally challenging (data quality, uncertainty)
10 - 35 minutes
- Explain the concepts of AI, machine learning, and deep learning
- Introduce supervised vs unsupervised learning
- Map learning paradigms to healthcare tasks (diagnosis, prognosis, patient stratification)
35 - 60 minutes
- Present main healthcare data types (EHR, imaging, time series, omics)
- Explain key characteristics (structure, dimensionality, noise, missingness)
- Interactive: students classify example problems into task types
60 - 80 minutes
- Introduce major model families (linear models, tree-based models, neural networks)
- Explain their assumptions and typical use cases
- Relate models to healthcare data modalities
80 - 100 minutes
- Explain evaluation concepts (train/test split, generalization, overfitting)
- Introduce performance metrics (accuracy, AUROC, precision/recall)
- Discuss healthcare-specific challenges (class imbalance, label noise, dataset shift)
100 - 115 minutes
- Present a simplified flawed healthcare AI example
- Interactive discussion: identify problems (bias, overfitting, poor validation)
- Emphasize limitations and risks of AI in healthcare
115 - 120 minutes
- Summarize key concepts (data -> task -> model -> evaluation -> limitation)
- Short Q&A

"When?	What?
0 - 10 minutes	
Introduction to the session: objectives, explanation of the workflow, importance of translating clinical needs into AI research questions; brief overview of the process (clinical problem → data → AI model → validation).
10 -45 minutes	Clinical case exploration and problem formulation: presentation of 1–2 clinical case studies (e.g., tumor detection, disease prediction); students identify the clinical problem, define the objective, and formulate a research question; guided discussion on possible AI approaches and data needs.
45 - 110 minutes	Interactive group activity: students work in small groups to design an AI-based solution; define data types, propose a model, identify challenges (bias, data limitations), and design a basic research protocol (dataset, validation, metrics); group presentations and discussion; role play (AI researcher, clinician, regulator) to evaluate feasibility and impact.
Last 10 minutes
Short wrap-up for the lesson: summary of key steps (problem → data → model → protocol), main challenges (bias, data, validation), and key take-home messages.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
5 minutes: Introduction to workshop format
Briefly recap high-risk classification logic (assumed prior knowledge).
Case-based legal reasoning and structured qualification.
Explain workflow: short input → case analysis → plenary discussion.
10 minutes: Key Concepts Refresher (Targeted)
Annex III catalogue: sector-specific high-risk use cases (e.g. employment, law enforcement, education).
Filter conditions: exclusion where system does not pose significant risk of harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights.
Intended purpose (as defined by provider).
Reasonably foreseeable misuse (objective standard).
NLF logic: harmonised conformity assessment and CE-marking framework.
40 minutes (or more): Case Work – examples:
Case Study 1 – Annex III Qualification
* Scenario: AI system used for CV screening in recruitment.
 * Tasks for students:
* Identify relevant Annex III category (employment).
   * Determine whether system qualifies as high-risk per se.
   * Discuss borderline issues (decision-support vs. decision-making).
 * Expected outcome: classification as high-risk AI system.
Case Study 2 – Application of Filter Conditions
* Scenario: AI system ranking job applicants based on non-decisive recommendations.
 * Tasks:
* Apply filter conditions:
* Does the system materially influence decisions?
     * Is there a significant risk to fundamental rights?
   * Evaluate whether exclusion from high-risk category is justified.
 * Focus: Burden of proof and documentation requirements.
Case Study 3 – Intended Purpose and Misuse
* Scenario: AI tool marketed for educational support, later used for student performance evaluation.
 * Tasks:
* Identify divergence between intended purpose and actual use.
   * Assess reasonably foreseeable misuse.
   * Determine classification consequences.
 * Key insight: classification depends on objective functional use, not only declared purpose.
Case Study 4 – NLF and Conformity Assessment
* Scenario: High-risk AI system integrated into a medical device.
 * Tasks:
* Identify applicable conformity assessment pathway.
   * Discuss role of notified bodies and harmonised standards.
 * AI Act builds on existing product safety architecture (NLF).
5 minutes: Plenary Discussion and Synthesis
Compare classification outcomes across groups.
Highlight common errors:
* Over-reliance on provider statements
 * Misapplication of filter conditions
Reinforce structured approach:
* Annex III applicability
 * Filter conditions
 * Contextual use and misuse
 * Compliance implications

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Tool: Scopus/Web of Science database, VOSviewer (latest version). 
Note: This is a computer practice session. Students must have active Scopus/WoS institutional access and have VOSviewer pre-installed on their workstations.
Instructions for teachers:
1.	Introduction (5 min): The instructor displays a high-resolution VOSviewer map from a recent study in sociology or media. Prompt for students: What patterns do you observe? Discuss the semantics of the visualization: node size (frequency/impact), edge thickness (link strength), and color-coded clusters (thematic or social proximity). 
2.	Conceptual Briefing (10 min): Define bibliometrics and its role in systematic literature reviews and state-of-the-art mapping. Distinguish between descriptive bibliometrics (productivity metrics, citation counts) and science mapping (structural relationships and intellectual evolution). Introduce the specific networks to be built: Co-authorship (social structure) and Keyword Co-occurrence (intellectual structure). Define VOSviewer parameters: nodes, edges, total link strength, clusters, and the minimum occurrence threshold. 
3.	Technical Demo (5 min): Demonstrate advanced data harvesting: building a query using Boolean operators (AND, OR, LIMIT-TO) and exporting metadata in CSV or RIS formats with full bibliographical information. 
4.	Data Collection (15 min): Students work individually or in pairs to define a research niche. They select a topic within media/culture (e.g., algorithmic bias, digital disinformation, platform labor, or AI in journalism). Students refine their queries to achieve a manageable corpus (300–800 records) to ensure visual clarity. 
5.	Descriptive Analysis (10 min): Using the database’s built-in "Analyze Results" tool, students report on the distribution of publications by year, top journals, and leading geographic regions.
6.	Science Mapping Practice (25 min): Students import their data into VOSviewer. They must generate two distinct maps: a co-authorship network and a keyword co-occurrence map. 
7.	Interpretation & Reporting (15 min): Students draft a brief report summarizing the primary research clusters and identifying the most influential nodes (authors or concepts) based on link strength. 
8.	Reflection and Sharing (15 min): Selected pairs present their maps.
9.	 Wrap-up (5 min): Summarize the key concepts and allow time for final questions. Homework: run the same query in both Scopus and Web of Science. Compare the resulting VOSviewer maps: are the thematic clusters consistent across databases?

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Tools: NodeXL. Gephi
Note: Students can have Gephi/NodeXL pre-installed on their notebooks.
Instructions for teachers:
1.	Introduction (5 min): The "Network Turn" in Social Sciences. Why connectivity often matters more than individual content in the digital age
2.	Conceptualizing the network (15 min): actors (nodes), relations (edges/ties), and attributes. Taxonomies of ties: directed vs. undirected, binary vs. weighted.
3.	Foundational Concepts (15 min): Introduce basic graph terminology. Discuss seminal studies: Jacob Moreno’s Sociometry, Mark Granovetter’s "Strength of Weak Ties" (information diffusion), and Manuel Castells’ "Network Society" as it pertains to contemporary media structures.
4.	Micro-discussion (10 min): Collaborative Mapping. In pairs, students select a specific media ecosystem (e.g., a newsroom hierarchy, a Twitter/X discourse community, or a podcast network) and sketch a graph with 5–7 nodes. Presentation of maps: Address the ontological question - what constitutes an "actor" in a media network? (Users, hashtags, bots, or media outlets).
5.	Core Metrics (15 min): Quantitative Interpretation of nodes. Degree centrality: popularity and immediate reach. Betweenness centrality: control over information flow and brokerage. Closeness centrality: efficiency and speed of access to the whole network.
6.	Network-Level Properties: Explain density, diameter, average path length (small world phenomenon), and clustering coefficient as the macro-context for interpretation.
7.	Applied Exercise (15 min): Manual calculation. Students compute degree and betweenness for a provided 7-node graph (on whiteboard or handout). Compare manual results with software output (Gephi/NodeXL) to demystify algorithmic calculations.
8.	Advanced Topology (10 min): Social Structures in Media. Clusters & Modularity: Identifying echo chambers, filter bubbles, and polarized discourse. Structural Holes (Ronald Burt): The role of the "broker" as a bridge between disconnected audiences. Opinion leaders vs. Bridge-builders in the digital landscape.
9.	Case-Study Analysis (15 min): Analyzing a real-world media campaign graph (pre-processed in Gephi, based on a familiar socio-political context). Task: Identify at least two distinct clusters; locate a node occupying a structural hole (broker); identify the top two opinion leaders. Justify each finding with the appropriate metric. Small group work followed by a brief plenary session.
10.	Conclusion & Reflection (5 min): One-sentence synthesis: "The most significant insight I gained today regarding media space through the lens of SNA is..."Synthesize student responses into the three core learning outcomes to reinforce the day's curriculum.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture examines disinformation as an economic system: the financial incentives of the attention economy, the ad-tech machinery that pays for engagement, and the way AI has lowered the cost of producing content optimised for clicks rather than accuracy. It is written for a Master's student training as an AI-driven communication and media specialist, so it treats disinformation not only as a content problem but as a supply chain with money at every step. The guiding question is who pays for this, and how.
Summary statement:
The lecture moves from the logic of the attention economy to the plumbing of programmatic advertising to the effect of generative AI, and then to the responses. It starts with Simon's account of attention as the scarce resource and the evidence that engagement and accuracy pull apart, using the Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (2018) study of false-news spread and its documented limits. It then explains how programmatic advertising works, through real-time bidding across exchanges and demand-side and supply-side platforms, and why automated placement, indifferent to site quality, routes advertiser money to made-for-advertising and disinformation sites, at a scale the Association of National Advertisers measures in the tens of billions of dollars. It shows how generative AI has turned this into an industrial process, with thousands of AI content farms built to harvest ad revenue, and how reputable brands end up funding them without knowing. It closes on the countermeasures and their limits.
Mission:
The module prepares communication professionals to reason about the money behind information. Students learn to follow the flow of advertising revenue from a brand's media budget to a disinformation publisher, to name the actors and mechanisms at each step, and to judge the countermeasures honestly, including why demonetisation is politically fraught and why several of its main implementers have pulled back under legal and political pressure. They then apply the EU frame: the Digital Services Act and the Code of Practice on Disinformation, now a Code of Conduct under Article 45, which carries advertising-transparency, recommender-system and demonetisation commitments. The applied work mirrors the day-to-day task of an AI-driven communication and media specialist: deciding where a brand's or an institution's advertising may run, how to set brand-safety and inclusion rules, and how to defend those decisions when the marketplace is opaque. The teaching aim is judgement about incentives: content moderation alone does not touch the business model, and changing what gets funded is a different and harder lever.
Session flow (90 minutes):
0 to 15, the attention economy: attention as the scarce resource (Simon), engagement as the currency, and why optimising for engagement diverges from accuracy; the Vosoughi et al. (2018) evidence and its limits.
15 to 40, the ad-tech machine: real-time bidding, exchanges, demand-side and supply-side platforms; made-for-advertising sites; why automated placement ignores site quality; the scale of wasted spend (ANA).
40 to 60, generative AI as an accelerant: AI content farms built for ad revenue (NewsGuard tracking since 2023); how ad money reaches disinformation publishers, and how a brand's ads end up on those sites through opaque programmatic buying rather than by choice; Google and the major exchanges are the largest single sources.
60 to 75, responses and their limits: demonetisation and follow-the-money (the Global Disinformation Index, Check My Ads, brand-safety), why it is contested, and its retreat under pressure; the EU frame (the Digital Services Act and the Code of Conduct on Disinformation).
75 to 90, applied exercise: in small groups, students trace the ad-revenue path for a given disinformation or AI-content-farm site, then draft a brand-safety and ad-placement policy for a named advertiser or public institution, and defend it against the transparency limits of the mark

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture examines the psychology of synthetic media: how AI-generated video, audio, images, and text change what audiences trust, how they judge what is real, and how public communication works when any recording can be challenged as fake. It is written for a Master's student training as an AI-driven communication and media specialist, so it treats synthetic media as a shift in the conditions of belief, not as a detection problem to be solved with a better tool. The lecture is built around the liar's dividend: once convincing fakes are common, the mere possibility of a fake lets a speaker dismiss authentic evidence as fabricated.
Summary statement:
The lecture moves from definitions to cognition to consequences to practice. It first separates deepfakes from cheapfakes and other manipulations and establishes that audiences react to the claim made about a piece of content more than to the technique behind it. It then explains the cognitive mechanisms that make synthetic content believable or persistent: the truth-default, the illusory-truth (repetition) effect, source-monitoring failure, and motivated reasoning. It then turns to the effects that matter most for a communicator. Current evidence indicates that political deepfakes are not, on average, more persuasive than other forms of misinformation, but that they destabilise trust in news and institutions and can damage the reputation of the person shown even when audiences rate the clip as not credible. The liar's dividend is presented as the sharpest form of this problem, with the experimental evidence for it and the current debate about how far it reaches video.
Mission:
The module prepares communication professionals to work in an environment where authenticity can no longer be inferred from the medium. Students examine how repetition, reliance on social media, and motivated reasoning shape belief, why credibility ratings understate the real harm of synthetic content, and how the liar's dividend is used to avoid accountability. They then build a practical response: a verification and disclosure workflow that relies on content provenance (C2PA content credentials) and plausibility-aware checking rather than on detection alone, that meets the transparency and labelling duties of Article 50 of the EU AI Act, and that communicates uncertainty without pushing audiences into indiscriminate distrust. The applied work mirrors the day-to-day task of an AI-driven communication and media specialist: deciding under time pressure whether to publish, label, or challenge a piece of media, and explaining that decision to an audience. The teaching aim is judgement: understanding what synthetic media does to an audience, and choosing communication practices that hold up when any single piece of evidence can be called fake.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Introduce the topic and explain its importance for organisational digital transformation
Explain that digital transformation is not only about introducing new technologies, but also about rethinking workflows, information flows, and the way value is created
Explain what process mapping and value-stream mapping are
Clarify the difference between simply describing a sequence of actions and analysing which stages actually create value for the user, client, or organisation
Show that a value stream includes operations, waiting time, information transfer, delays, and losses
Review the main elements of a process map and a value-stream map: start and end of the process, stages, actors, information flows, completion time, waiting, handoffs, and outputs
Explain how to document the current state of a process and why this is the basis for meaningful improvement
Explain how mapping helps identify problem areas, such as unnecessary steps, duplication of actions, repeated data entry, delays, gaps between units, and overdependence on manual work
Provide a short example of a process where digital transformation should begin with understanding the current state rather than immediately introducing a new tool
Explain how AI tools can support process and value-stream mapping
Discuss examples of using AI to summarise textual descriptions of a process, turn notes into a structured sequence of stages, identify recurring problems, group types of waste, and support initial analytical preparation for process mapping
Emphasise that AI can accelerate analysis, but it does not replace collective understanding of the workflow or professional judgement
Introduce the concepts of current-state and future-state mapping
Explain how the current-state map can be used to define desirable improvements, digital intervention points, new coordination patterns, and ways to reduce waste
Stress that the future state should not simply be “more digital”, but more logical, faster, clearer, and more value-oriented
Discuss criteria for evaluating process quality in the context of digital transformation, including speed, continuity, transparency, user convenience, reduction of waste, quality of information transfer, scalability, and digital support
Briefly review the risks of superficial transformation, when digital tools are placed on top of an inefficient process without real redesign
Practical activity.
Learners work in groups on a short workflow that requires digital transformation, for example document approval, request processing, internal application review, public service delivery, or information exchange between units
Each group should outline the current state of the process, identify value-adding and non-value-adding stages, detect waste or delays, and propose a future-state version of the process
Groups may use free digital whiteboards or simple visual tools to build the map
In addition, groups may use AI tools to organise the process description, summarise problem points, or generate an initial list of possible improvements
Hold short presentations of group results
Discuss which types of waste and inefficiencies were identified, how realistic the future-state design is, and how the proposed changes support digital transformation
Wrap up the lesson
Emphasise that process and value-stream mapping are practical tools of digital transformation, and that combining visualisation, team analysis, and appropriate use of AI supports more informed decisions about process improvement

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
1.	Introduce the topic by asking why a small AI prototype may look cheap but become expensive when scaled across the organisation. Explain that AI economics is about understanding the costs, benefits, and trade-offs involved in building, buying, and operating AI systems.
2.	Explain tokenomics as the cost structure of using generative AI systems through tokens. A token is a small unit of text processed by a model. Both input and output usually count towards cost. Longer prompts, larger documents, longer responses, repeated queries, and bigger context windows all increase cost.
3.	Clarify the main cost drivers:
(a) Input tokens: the text sent to the model.
(b) Output tokens: the text generated by the model.
(c) Model choice: larger or more capable models usually cost more.
(d) Context length: long documents or conversations increase processing cost.
(e) Frequency of use: repeated use across many users multiplies cost.
(f) Latency and performance requirements: faster or higher-reliability systems may cost more.
(g) Human review: many AI outputs still require checking, approval, or correction.
(h) Integration and governance: security, monitoring, compliance, maintenance, and vendor management add cost.
4.	Use a simple example. A chatbot that costs only a few cents per conversation may seem cheap. However, if thousands of employees use it daily with long prompts and long outputs, the monthly cost can become significant. The business case must consider unit cost, volume, value per use, and risk.
5.	Explain the difference between three levels of AI economics:
(a) Prototype economics: small-scale, experimental, and low usage.
(b) Production economics: high-volume, monitored, governed, integrated, and continuously improved.
(c) Enterprise economics: includes training, compliance, support, vendor management, security, change management, and long-term maintenance.
6.	Introduce a simple economic assessment framework:
(a) What task is the AI performing?
(b) How often will it be used?
(c) How many tokens are used per interaction?
(d) Which model is required?
(e) What is the cost per use?
(f) What human review is needed?
(g) What time, cost, or quality benefit is created?
(h) Does the benefit justify the operating cost at scale?
7.	Discuss ways to manage cost. These may include using shorter prompts, limiting unnecessary output, using smaller models for simpler tasks, caching repeated answers, summarising documents before analysis, routing complex tasks only to advanced models, and monitoring usage by team or use case.
8.	Emphasise that the cheapest model is not always the best choice. A cheaper model may produce lower-quality outputs, require more human correction, or create business risk. The goal is not simply cost reduction, but value-for-money.
9.	Suggested Classroom Activity.
Ask groups to choose one AI use case, such as customer support, document summarisation, legal review, internal knowledge search, coding support, or report drafting. Each group should define the AI task, expected number of users, frequency of use, likely input and output size, model choice, main cost drivers, expected business benefit, risks and hidden costs, and ways to reduce cost while preserving value.
10.	Closing Message.
AI tokenomics helps organisations understand the real cost of using generative AI at scale. Good AI economics connects technical design with business value, ensuring that AI systems are not only impressive but also sustainable and cost-effective.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Tool: Scopus/Web of Science database, VOSviewer (latest version). 
Note: This is a computer practice session. Students must have active Scopus/WoS institutional access and have VOSviewer pre-installed on their workstations.
Instructions for teachers:
1.	Introduction (5 min): The instructor displays a high-resolution VOSviewer map from a recent study in sociology or media. Prompt for students: What patterns do you observe? Discuss the semantics of the visualization: node size (frequency/impact), edge thickness (link strength), and color-coded clusters (thematic or social proximity). 
2.	Conceptual Briefing (10 min): Define bibliometrics and its role in systematic literature reviews and state-of-the-art mapping. Distinguish between descriptive bibliometrics (productivity metrics, citation counts) and science mapping (structural relationships and intellectual evolution). Introduce the specific networks to be built: Co-authorship (social structure) and Keyword Co-occurrence (intellectual structure). Define VOSviewer parameters: nodes, edges, total link strength, clusters, and the minimum occurrence threshold. 
3.	Technical Demo (5 min): Demonstrate advanced data harvesting: building a query using Boolean operators (AND, OR, LIMIT-TO) and exporting metadata in CSV or RIS formats with full bibliographical information. 
4.	Data Collection (15 min): Students work individually or in pairs to define a research niche. They select a topic within media/culture (e.g., algorithmic bias, digital disinformation, platform labor, or AI in journalism). Students refine their queries to achieve a manageable corpus (300–800 records) to ensure visual clarity. 
5.	Descriptive Analysis (10 min): Using the database’s built-in "Analyze Results" tool, students report on the distribution of publications by year, top journals, and leading geographic regions.
6.	Science Mapping Practice (25 min): Students import their data into VOSviewer. They must generate two distinct maps: a co-authorship network and a keyword co-occurrence map. 
7.	Interpretation & Reporting (15 min): Students draft a brief report summarizing the primary research clusters and identifying the most influential nodes (authors or concepts) based on link strength. 
8.	Reflection and Sharing (15 min): Selected pairs present their maps.
9.	 Wrap-up (5 min): Summarize the key concepts and allow time for final questions. Homework: run the same query in both Scopus and Web of Science. Compare the resulting VOSviewer maps: are the thematic clusters consistent across databases?

Instructions for teachers:
1.	Introduction (5 min): The "Network Turn" in Social Sciences. Why connectivity often matters more than individual content in the digital age
2.	Conceptualizing the network (15 min): actors (nodes), relations (edges/ties), and attributes. Taxonomies of ties: directed vs. undirected, binary vs. weighted.
3.	Foundational Concepts (15 min): Introduce basic graph terminology. Discuss seminal studies: Jacob Moreno’s Sociometry, Mark Granovetter’s "Strength of Weak Ties" (information diffusion), and Manuel Castells’ "Network Society" as it pertains to contemporary media structures.
4.	Micro-discussion (10 min): Collaborative Mapping. In pairs, students select a specific media ecosystem (e.g., a newsroom hierarchy, a Twitter/X discourse community, or a podcast network) and sketch a graph with 5–7 nodes. Presentation of maps: Address the ontological question - what constitutes an "actor" in a media network? (Users, hashtags, bots, or media outlets).
5.	Core Metrics (15 min): Quantitative Interpretation of nodes. Degree centrality: popularity and immediate reach. Betweenness centrality: control over information flow and brokerage. Closeness centrality: efficiency and speed of access to the whole network.
6.	Network-Level Properties: Explain density, diameter, average path length (small world phenomenon), and clustering coefficient as the macro-context for interpretation.
7.	Applied Exercise (15 min): Manual calculation. Students compute degree and betweenness for a provided 7-node graph (on whiteboard or handout). Compare manual results with software output (Gephi/NodeXL) to demystify algorithmic calculations.
8.	Advanced Topology (10 min): Social Structures in Media. Clusters & Modularity: Identifying echo chambers, filter bubbles, and polarized discourse. Structural Holes (Ronald Burt): The role of the "broker" as a bridge between disconnected audiences. Opinion leaders vs. Bridge-builders in the digital landscape.
9.	Case-Study Analysis (15 min): Analyzing a real-world media campaign graph (pre-processed in Gephi, based on a familiar socio-political context). Task: Identify at least two distinct clusters; locate a node occupying a structural hole (broker); identify the top two opinion leaders. Justify each finding with the appropriate metric. Small group work followed by a brief plenary session.
10.	Conclusion & Reflection (5 min): One-sentence synthesis: "The most significant insight I gained today regarding media space through the lens of SNA is..."Synthesize student responses into the three core learning outcomes to reinforce the day's curriculum.

* Scenario: AI system used for CV screening in recruitment.

* Does the system materially influence decisions?

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture examines disinformation as an economic system: the financial incentives of the attention economy, the ad-tech machinery that pays for engagement, and the way AI has lowered the cost of producing content optimised for clicks rather than accuracy. It is written for a Master's student training as an AI-driven communication and media specialist, so it treats disinformation not only as a content problem but as a supply chain with money at every step. The guiding question is who pays for this, and how.
Summary statement:
The lecture moves from the logic of the attention economy to the plumbing of programmatic advertising to the effect of generative AI, and then to the responses. It starts with Simon's account of attention as the scarce resource and the evidence that engagement and accuracy pull apart, using the Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (2018) study of false-news spread and its documented limits. It then explains how programmatic advertising works, through real-time bidding across exchanges and demand-side and supply-side platforms, and why automated placement, indifferent to site quality, routes advertiser money to made-for-advertising and disinformation sites, at a scale the Association of National Advertisers measures in the tens of billions of dollars. It shows how generative AI has turned this into an industrial process, with thousands of AI content farms built to harvest ad revenue, and how reputable brands end up funding them without knowing. It closes on the countermeasures and their limits.
Mission:
The module prepares communication professionals to reason about the money behind information. Students learn to follow the flow of advertising revenue from a brand's media budget to a disinformation publisher, to name the actors and mechanisms at each step, and to judge the countermeasures honestly, including why demonetisation is politically fraught and why several of its main implementers have pulled back under legal and political pressure. They then apply the EU frame: the Digital Services Act and the Code of Practice on Disinformation, now a Code of Conduct under Article 45, which carries advertising-transparency, recommender-system and demonetisation commitments. The applied work mirrors the day-to-day task of an AI-driven communication and media specialist: deciding where a brand's or an institution's advertising may run, how to set brand-safety and inclusion rules, and how to defend those decisions when the marketplace is opaque. The teaching aim is judgement about incentives: content moderation alone does not touch the business model, and changing what gets funded is a different and harder lever.
Session flow (90 minutes):
0 to 15, the attention economy: attention as the scarce resource (Simon), engagement as the currency, and why optimising for engagement diverges from accuracy; the Vosoughi et al. (2018) evidence and its limits.
15 to 40, the ad-tech machine: real-time bidding, exchanges, demand-side and supply-side platforms; made-for-advertising sites; why automated placement ignores site quality; the scale of wasted spend (ANA).
40 to 60, generative AI as an accelerant: AI content farms built for ad revenue (NewsGuard tracking since 2023); how ad money reaches disinformation publishers, and how a brand's ads end up on those sites through opaque programmatic buying rather than by choice; Google and the major exchanges are the largest single sources.
60 to 75, responses and their limits: demonetisation and follow-the-money (the Global Disinformation Index, Check My Ads, brand-safety), why it is contested, and its retreat under pressure; the EU frame (the Digital Services Act and the Code of Conduct on Disinformation).
75 to 90, applied exercise: in small groups, students trace the ad-revenue path for a given disinformation or AI-content-farm site, then draft a brand-safety and ad-placement policy for a named advertiser or public institution, and defend it against the transparency limits of the mark

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
This 90-minute lecture examines the psychology of synthetic media: how AI-generated video, audio, images, and text change what audiences trust, how they judge what is real, and how public communication works when any recording can be challenged as fake. It is written for a Master's student training as an AI-driven communication and media specialist, so it treats synthetic media as a shift in the conditions of belief, not as a detection problem to be solved with a better tool. The lecture is built around the liar's dividend: once convincing fakes are common, the mere possibility of a fake lets a speaker dismiss authentic evidence as fabricated.
Summary statement:
The lecture moves from definitions to cognition to consequences to practice. It first separates deepfakes from cheapfakes and other manipulations and establishes that audiences react to the claim made about a piece of content more than to the technique behind it. It then explains the cognitive mechanisms that make synthetic content believable or persistent: the truth-default, the illusory-truth (repetition) effect, source-monitoring failure, and motivated reasoning. It then turns to the effects that matter most for a communicator. Current evidence indicates that political deepfakes are not, on average, more persuasive than other forms of misinformation, but that they destabilise trust in news and institutions and can damage the reputation of the person shown even when audiences rate the clip as not credible. The liar's dividend is presented as the sharpest form of this problem, with the experimental evidence for it and the current debate about how far it reaches video.
Mission:
The module prepares communication professionals to work in an environment where authenticity can no longer be inferred from the medium. Students examine how repetition, reliance on social media, and motivated reasoning shape belief, why credibility ratings understate the real harm of synthetic content, and how the liar's dividend is used to avoid accountability. They then build a practical response: a verification and disclosure workflow that relies on content provenance (C2PA content credentials) and plausibility-aware checking rather than on detection alone, that meets the transparency and labelling duties of Article 50 of the EU AI Act, and that communicates uncertainty without pushing audiences into indiscriminate distrust. The applied work mirrors the day-to-day task of an AI-driven communication and media specialist: deciding under time pressure whether to publish, label, or challenge a piece of media, and explaining that decision to an audience. The teaching aim is judgement: understanding what synthetic media does to an audience, and choosing communication practices that hold up when any single piece of evidence can be called fake.

0 to 15, definitions and taxonomy: deepfakes, cheapfakes, generated audio, image and text; why the claim attached to content matters more to audiences than the production method.

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open with the claim that strategy lives and dies in the operating model. An AI strategy the operating model cannot execute is a document, not a strategy, and the session exists to make the execution discipline visible and teachable.
Introduce the AI operating model archetypes. Define a centralised Centre of Excellence as the pattern in which AI capability is concentrated for leverage and consistency, a federated model as the pattern in which business units own their own AI capability for pace and relevance, and a hybrid model as the attempt to combine the two through a shared platform and distributed delivery. Walk through the decision logic that points to each archetype and show named examples from the banking, retail, and industrial sectors.
Move to RACI matrix design. Show how decision rights in AI systems span data stewards, model owners, business sponsors, and risk functions, and how a poorly designed RACI produces the characteristic AI failure mode of an incident with no accountable owner. Work through a RACI for an AI model that makes a materially impactful decision, and make the accountabilities concrete.
Cover process redesign for AI integration. Identify the human decision nodes that AI can inform, augment, or replace, and show how the redesign is not a one-to-one substitution but a rethinking of the process itself. Use a credit-decisioning or demand-forecasting example to make the redesign visible.
Address cross-functional teaming. Define the composition and charter of an effective AI product team: the technical lead, the domain expert, the risk representative, the product owner, and the business sponsor. Show how charter confusion produces team dysfunction and how explicit decision rights prevent it.
Close the content with change management. Role displacement, capability gaps, and resistance to new accountability structures are the predictable human responses to operating model redesign. Name the specific interventions, coaching, communication, and capability development, that the literature shows to be effective, and connect them to the work done in the Leadership workstream.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to architect a target operating model that specifies decision rights and the interface between centralised and federated functions, trace the dependencies between use cases, processes, and roles to identify where current choices will constrain scaling, and make a reasoned case for a CoE, federated, or hybrid pattern with explicit trade-offs in accountability and pace.
"

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open with the observation that most enterprise AI portfolios resemble a shopping list more than a strategy. The shopping-list portfolio has a technical name, a portfolio of point solutions without foundational investments, and the failure mode it produces is well documented and expensive.
Introduce AI project interdependencies and foundational-capability sequencing. Investments in data platforms, MLOps infrastructure, identity and access management, and model governance enable and gate downstream use cases. Show a concrete example where three downstream use cases all depended on the same absent foundational investment, and the portfolio delivered only one of them because the others were starved of the prerequisite. Introduce the sequencing discipline of quick wins, capability builders, and flagship transformations, arranged so that each phase unlocks the next.
Move to risk-adjusted portfolio scoring. Walk through a multi-criteria prioritisation matrix that incorporates technical debt, regulatory exposure, talent availability, data readiness, and strategic alignment. Show the weighting trade-offs that differ by industry and by the organisation's position on its maturity curve, and connect this to the maturity model work in BSAIC-16. Make explicit the difference between scoring for comparison and scoring for decision, and why the scoring instrument itself needs to be calibrated before it is trusted.
Address the staged investment logic. Quick wins build credibility and release resources, capability builders remove the foundational constraints that gate the rest of the portfolio, and flagship transformations deliver the strategic intent. Show how mis-sequencing produces programme failure even when each individual project is well managed.
Explore the communication discipline. Translating a technical sequencing logic into a Board-ready investment narrative is a specialist act. Walk through the narrative structure: the strategic frame, the dependency map, the staged investment ask, and the forward-looking risk posture. Contrast this with the project-by-project approval pattern that produces portfolio incoherence.
Close the content with the failure modes. Approving point solutions without their prerequisites, neglecting dependencies, under-investing in foundational capabilities, and substituting a list of initiatives for a coherent roadmap. Name each and the specific preventive discipline.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to curate a risk-adjusted portfolio that sequences quick wins, capability builders, and flagship transformations, rank-order initiatives against a defensible multi-criteria instrument, trace foundational dependencies and diagnose the point-solution failure mode, and communicate the roadmap to a simulated Board as an investment narrative that survives cross-examination.
"

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
Open by naming the central design choice. Every AI deployment makes a decision about where humans and machines sit on the work, and most organisations make that decision implicitly, by default, rather than by design. The session exists to make it a deliberate act.
Introduce the augmentation-automation spectrum. Define augmentation as AI supporting a human whose judgement remains primary, and automation as AI executing without routine human involvement. Anchor the discussion in the theoretical foundations from Brynjolfsson and McAfee, and show how current enterprise practice has evolved the spectrum into a more granular set of design patterns.
Move to task decomposition methodology. Show how a role breaks down into tasks, and each task into subtasks, and how each subtask can be assessed for where value sits on the human-machine boundary. Use a knowledge-work role, legal document review, radiology, or financial analysis, and walk through the decomposition in detail. Make the exercise concrete, not theoretical.
Introduce cognitive load theory as the design constraint that most human-AI systems ignore. Working memory is finite, and poorly designed AI interfaces overwhelm practitioners with alerts, recommendations, and probabilistic scores that cannot be usefully integrated. Show how interfaces that respect cognitive load, by summarising rather than streaming and by prioritising rather than enumerating, produce measurably better outcomes.
Work through organisational case studies. Radiological diagnosis, where AI augments the radiologist's reading, legal document review, where AI pre-filters and classifies, and financial analysis, where AI triangulates signals across noisy sources. Make clear what worked, what did not, and what the design choices were that differentiated the outcomes.
Close the content with measurement. Productivity metrics alone are insufficient because they miss decision quality and practitioner wellbeing. Walk through the full measurement stack and show why a single-metric view produces gaming and burnout, both of which defeat the deployment's original purpose.
Finish with a crisp action summary: participants should leave able to deconstruct a knowledge-work role into its constituent tasks and map each against the augmentation-automation spectrum with reference to complementarity and cognitive-load evidence, design a human-AI dyad that specifies task division, support form, and oversight interface, and contest the implicit assumptions behind a proposed automation design about where value and risk sit on the human-machine boundary.
"

Introduce the topic and explain its importance for organisational digital transformation
Explain that digital transformation is not only about introducing new technologies, but also about rethinking workflows, information flows, and the way value is created
Explain what process mapping and value-stream mapping are
Clarify the difference between simply describing a sequence of actions and analysing which stages actually create value for the user, client, or organisation
Show that a value stream includes operations, waiting time, information transfer, delays, and losses
Review the main elements of a process map and a value-stream map: start and end of the process, stages, actors, information flows, completion time, waiting, handoffs, and outputs
Explain how to document the current state of a process and why this is the basis for meaningful improvement
Explain how mapping helps identify problem areas, such as unnecessary steps, duplication of actions, repeated data entry, delays, gaps between units, and overdependence on manual work
Provide a short example of a process where digital transformation should begin with understanding the current state rather than immediately introducing a new tool
Explain how AI tools can support process and value-stream mapping
Discuss examples of using AI to summarise textual descriptions of a process, turn notes into a structured sequence of stages, identify recurring problems, group types of waste, and support initial analytical preparation for process mapping
Emphasise that AI can accelerate analysis, but it does not replace collective understanding of the workflow or professional judgement
Introduce the concepts of current-state and future-state mapping
Explain how the current-state map can be used to define desirable improvements, digital intervention points, new coordination patterns, and ways to reduce waste
Stress that the future state should not simply be “more digital”, but more logical, faster, clearer, and more value-oriented
Discuss criteria for evaluating process quality in the context of digital transformation, including speed, continuity, transparency, user convenience, reduction of waste, quality of information transfer, scalability, and digital support
Briefly review the risks of superficial transformation, when digital tools are placed on top of an inefficient process without real redesign
Practical activity.
Learners work in groups on a short workflow that requires digital transformation, for example document approval, request processing, internal application review, public service delivery, or information exchange between units
Each group should outline the current state of the process, identify value-adding and non-value-adding stages, detect waste or delays, and propose a future-state version of the process
Groups may use free digital whiteboards or simple visual tools to build the map
In addition, groups may use AI tools to organise the process description, summarise problem points, or generate an initial list of possible improvements
Hold short presentations of group results
Discuss which types of waste and inefficiencies were identified, how realistic the future-state design is, and how the proposed changes support digital transformation
Wrap up the lesson
Emphasise that process and value-stream mapping are practical tools of digital transformation, and that combining visualisation, team analysis, and appropriate use of AI supports more informed decisions about process improvement

wiki_sections.name: Instructions for teachers
wiki_sections.text:
1.	Introduce the topic by asking why a small AI prototype may look cheap but become expensive when scaled across the organisation. Explain that AI economics is about understanding the costs, benefits, and trade-offs involved in building, buying, and operating AI systems.
2.	Explain tokenomics as the cost structure of using generative AI systems through tokens. A token is a small unit of text processed by a model. Both input and output usually count towards cost. Longer prompts, larger documents, longer responses, repeated queries, and bigger context windows all increase cost.
3.	Clarify the main cost drivers:
(a) Input tokens: the text sent to the model.
(b) Output tokens: the text generated by the model.
(c) Model choice: larger or more capable models usually cost more.
(d) Context length: long documents or conversations increase processing cost.
(e) Frequency of use: repeated use across many users multiplies cost.
(f) Latency and performance requirements: faster or higher-reliability systems may cost more.
(g) Human review: many AI outputs still require checking, approval, or correction.
(h) Integration and governance: security, monitoring, compliance, maintenance, and vendor management add cost.
4.	Use a simple example. A chatbot that costs only a few cents per conversation may seem cheap. However, if thousands of employees use it daily with long prompts and long outputs, the monthly cost can become significant. The business case must consider unit cost, volume, value per use, and risk.
5.	Explain the difference between three levels of AI economics:
(a) Prototype economics: small-scale, experimental, and low usage.
(b) Production economics: high-volume, monitored, governed, integrated, and continuously improved.
(c) Enterprise economics: includes training, compliance, support, vendor management, security, change management, and long-term maintenance.
6.	Introduce a simple economic assessment framework:
(a) What task is the AI performing?
(b) How often will it be used?
(c) How many tokens are used per interaction?
(d) Which model is required?
(e) What is the cost per use?
(f) What human review is needed?
(g) What time, cost, or quality benefit is created?
(h) Does the benefit justify the operating cost at scale?
7.	Discuss ways to manage cost. These may include using shorter prompts, limiting unnecessary output, using smaller models for simpler tasks, caching repeated answers, summarising documents before analysis, routing complex tasks only to advanced models, and monitoring usage by team or use case.
8.	Emphasise that the cheapest model is not always the best choice. A cheaper model may produce lower-quality outputs, require more human correction, or create business risk. The goal is not simply cost reduction, but value-for-money.
9.	Suggested Classroom Activity.
Ask groups to choose one AI use case, such as customer support, document summarisation, legal review, internal knowledge search, coding support, or report drafting. Each group should define the AI task, expected number of users, frequency of use, likely input and output size, model choice, main cost drivers, expected business benefit, risks and hidden costs, and ways to reduce cost while preserving value.
10.	Closing Message.
AI tokenomics helps organisations understand the real cost of using generative AI at scale. Good AI economics connects technical design with business value, ensuring that AI systems are not only impressive but also sustainable and cost-effective.
